summary:
Calzone: look at your plate, know what’s in it. We built Calzone, a nutrition-tracking feature in our HelloVitals health-monitoring app for iPhone, Mac and Meta smart glasses. A crew member looks at a meal through the glasses, takes a photo, or uploads one. An AI model running on our own computer (MedGemma, by Google) names each food and estimates portions. The astronaut checks and corrects them, and Calzone looks up every food in the USDA food database. It shows calories and 22 nutrients against Earth’s daily needs (FDA) and NASA’s spaceflight requirements (JSC-67378). It flags spaceflight risks, like low vitamin D or iron near NASA’s limit, and keeps a daily total.

This matters because NASA studies found astronauts ate only about 80% of the energy they needed, and their vitamin D dropped even with supplements. On a mission to Mars there is no dietitian on board, so the crew must monitor itself. Calzone works offline, never invents numbers (every value comes from the USDA database), and keeps photos private. In our test, it correctly identified 10 of 13 foods.
details:
What it does and how it works

Calzone is a nutrition-tracking feature in HelloVitals, our crew health-monitoring app. A crew member captures a meal in one of three ways: they look at it through Meta smart glasses, take a photo with the iPhone, or upload up to five photos.

  1. An AI vision model running on our own Mac (MedGemma 1.5 4B, by Google) names each food and estimates its weight.
  2. The crew member checks the list. They can swap a food for a closer match, fix the grams, or add anything the AI missed.
  3. Calzone looks up every food in the USDA FoodData Central database, stored offline with 7,793 foods.
  4. It shows calories and 22 nutrients, each as a percentage of Earth daily needs (FDA Daily Values) and NASA’s spaceflight requirements (JSC-67378). Values near a limit turn orange.
  5. Meals add up to a daily total, shared by the phone and the Mac web page.
  6. A “papers” button finds research on each nutrient through Google Scholar.

Benefits

  • Fast: each scan takes 1 to 8 seconds, much quicker than logging food by hand.
  • Space-specific: it shows where needs differ in flight. Vitamin D is higher (25 µg a day, because there’s no sunlight), and iron has a limit of 8 mg a day for most crew, because stored iron rises in flight.
  • Trustworthy: the AI only names foods. Every number comes from the USDA database, and each food links to its USDA entry.
  • Offline and private: it needs no internet, and photos are never saved.

Intended impact

NASA studies found astronauts on the International Space Station ate only about 80% of the energy they needed, and their vitamin D dropped even with supplements. On a mission to Mars, no dietitian is on board, so the crew has to be its own nutritionist. Calzone helps crews catch low calories, low vitamin D or too much iron early. The same tool also helps people on Earth understand their meals.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Swift and SwiftUI (iPhone app), Python (server), JavaScript, HTML and CSS (web page).
  • AI: MedGemma 1.5 4B, run locally with llama.cpp.
  • Data: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy). Targets from the FDA Daily Values and NASA JSC-67378.
  • Services: Meta Wearables Device Access Toolkit (glasses camera), Apple HealthKit (watch vitals in HelloVitals), Tailscale (secure phone-to-Mac link), and SerpApi (Google Scholar search).
  • Hardware: a Mac, an iPhone 17 Pro, an Apple Watch Series 11 and Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
  • Development tools: Xcode, Claude Code (an AI coding assistant), and ffmpeg plus ElevenLabs (an AI voice) for the demo video.

What makes it creative

It combines smart glasses, a phone and an offline AI so a crew member can check a meal just by looking at it. Each plate gets two answers side by side, one for Earth and one for space. That makes it clear that the same lunch can be fine on Earth but use half of NASA’s iron limit in space. The AI’s role is limited on purpose: it suggests foods, and people confirm them.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: we tested the AI ourselves, and it named 10 of 13 foods correctly. We show its mistakes openly instead of hiding them.
  • Safety: NASA’s iron rule changes for women under 50 who menstruate (they need at least 18 mg), and Calzone follows that exception.
  • Privacy and offline use: everything runs on our own computer, photos aren’t saved, and the phone needs a pairing code to connect.
  • Honesty: portion sizes from a photo are only guesses, and the app says it’s not medical advice.
  • Licensing and AI use: we used only openly licensed photos and public-domain data, and we disclose every AI tool we used.
dataRefs: NASA JSC-67378 Rev 1: Nutritional Requirements for Exploration Missions up to 365 Days (2020)
